questiontext.text:
🌾 Harvest Hunt: Investigating Variability

Explore a field of 100 plots using exactly 15 measurements. Click a grey square to reveal its crop yield. Plots sharing an edge differ by no more than 5 yield units.

After the fifteenth measurement, your observed range is recorded automatically and used as an estimate of the whole-field range. Then click REVEAL THE FULL FIELD to uncover all 100 plots and compare the two ranges. Your measured plots stay outlined in blue.

Your observed range from your 15 measured plots is shown in the field notes above and is recorded automatically. Are you within 5 yield units of the actual range?

generalfeedback.text:
The observed range is calculated from the 15 measured plots. It can never exceed the full-field range, because the most extreme values in a sample can be no more extreme than those in the whole field. The amount missed is the full-field range minus the observed range. In this field the highest and the lowest yields each occur in a single plot, so a sample of 15 can easily miss them, even though neighbouring plots differ by at most 5 units.

The statements in (b):

  • The full-field range could be smaller than my observed range. False: the sample range can never exceed the full-field range.
  • Measuring extra plots can never make the observed range smaller. True: a new plot either lies inside the current range or widens it.
  • Plots close together are likely to miss the extremes. True: neighbouring yields are similar, so clustered plots cover only a narrow band of values.
  • A sample range is equally likely to overestimate or underestimate. False: it can only underestimate the full-field range or match it exactly.
